content:
Camila Reyes: need to lock the *headline stats* for the benchmark report today. What’s the primary angle we want to lead with on landing page + press kit?

Ben Carter: sharing current draft hero options from wirecopy (Drive):
- A) “Latency per dollar: the production economics benchmark for LLM inference”
- B) “Lowest cost per 1M tokens across regions”
- C) “Fast + reliable open-model inference across regions”

Ben Carter: and draft headline stats block (not final):
1) “Up to 2.1× better latency/$ vs. common hosted configs”
2) “p95 latency under 900ms on chat baseline (NA/EU)”
3) “<0.2% error rate during benchmark windows”

Soojin Lee: gut: A is the differentiator. B is too procurement-y + invites pricing knife fight. C is generic unless we back it up. But we need to be really careful about what “vs” means.

Ethan Wallace: +1. The report is literally about production economics. If we lead with cost-only we undermine the narrative (latency + cost + ops). For the hero, can we frame as “benchmarking latency/$ across models + regions” without implying we win everything?

Claire Dubois: flagging: the “2.1×” is real in *some* model/region combos but not universal. Also depends on caching/batching settings. We can say “up to” but we must clearly define the comparison baseline (and that it’s our measured suite).

Jonas Weber: agree. Also reliability: the “<0.2% error rate” is for the harness + controlled windows. It’s not an SLA. We should not headline error rate IMO.

Tyler Benson: from attribution / ads POV, “latency/$” is distinctive and tests well (engineers click). “lowest cost” triggers “what about quality?” comments. If we keep a number in the hero, please give me a version that doesn’t get us into claim review hell.

Tessa Morgan: design POV: one hero metric is doable, two is crowded. If we lead with “latency/$” we can do a simple chart snippet + a short “how to read this” block.

Renee Sullivan: for social, “latency per dollar” is a new hook. If we instead say “cheapest,” replies will be “show receipts” + “depends on tokens/sec.” Better to lead with the concept + link to methodology.

Camila Reyes: ok so directionally: lead with latency/$ concept. Question: do we include a numeric claim in the hero at all?

Ben Carter: I’d like one number for conversion. But open to making it softer / contextual.

Michael Grant: looping in (legal). If we include a numeric claim in hero:
- must be qualified (e.g., “up to” + “in our benchmark suite”)
- must avoid unnamed competitor comparisons unless the baseline is clearly defined and not misleading
- must avoid implying general performance superiority across all workloads
- must include variance language somewhere above the fold or very near it (e.g., “results vary by model/region/workload; see methodology”)

Soojin Lee: what if hero is:
“Latency per dollar (ms/$) benchmark across open models and regions.”
Then subhead:
“See how throughput, p50/p95 latency, and cost interact in production-like workloads.”
Then first stat callout could be “Best-in-suite latency/$ observed: X ms/$ (Model Y, Region Z)” with a link to table.

Ethan Wallace: that’s safer and also nerdy in a good way. But “X ms/$” might confuse at a glance.

Claire Dubois: agreed, ms/$ is not intuitive. In the report we also compute “tokens/sec per $” as a supporting metric. But the whole point is “latency per dollar.” We can add a one-liner definition right next to it.

Jonas Weber: suggestion: keep the hero numeric as *range* not a win claim.
Example: “Latency/$ varies by ~1.6×–2.1× across regions for the same model/config in our suite” (if true). It highlights why benchmarking matters rather than “we are best.”

Ben Carter: I like the “why this matters” framing. But we need to check that range is accurate and doesn’t sound like we’re admitting inconsistency.

Tyler Benson: range framing is good for credibility. Also easier in ads: “Latency/$ varies a lot by region—here’s the data.” It’s an insight, not a chest-thump.

Tessa Morgan: UX: we can do a small callout card:
“Why latency/$: two deployments with the same $/1M tokens can feel *very* different in user experience.”
Then an example chart.

Camila Reyes: ok, so no “2.1× better than X” in the hero. Where do we use the 2.1× at all?

Ethan Wallace: we can keep “up to 2.1× better latency/$” inside the Findings section of the PDF *if* we define exactly what it compares (e.g., Redwood Hosted default profile vs baseline hosted config in our harness) + include table reference + variability disclaimer.

Michael Grant: that’s more acceptable if it’s (1) substantiated and (2) not framed as a general market claim. Also avoid “common hosted configs” unless we can prove what “common” is. Prefer: “relative to baseline configuration defined in Methodology §3.2”.

Soojin Lee: +1. “Common” is squishy.

Claire Dubois: I can provide the precise baseline definition text:
- same model version
- same prompt distribution + concurrency
- baseline runtime settings (batching on, caching policy X)
- prices from Redwood metering for the run window
We should not imply competitor pricing or infra.

Ben Carter: cool, I’ll revise.

Camila Reyes: what about reliability angle? Do we say anything up top?

Jonas Weber: we should include a caveat block near the top:
“Benchmarks reflect controlled run windows and include variance analysis; not an SLA.”
Reliability should show up as “guardrails + methodology,” not a headline claim.

Renee Sullivan: agree. For external comms, “reliability caveats” reads like “results are shaky.” Better: “Reproducible methodology + variance reported.”

Tyler Benson: we can also add “confidence bands / rerun policy” bullet in the FAQ.

Camila Reyes: decision:
1) Primary angle = latency/$ (production economics)
2) No competitor-ish numeric hero claim
3) Include methodology-first disclaimer near top (variance, not SLA)

Ben Carter: proposed hero copy v2:
Hero: “The latency-per-dollar benchmark for LLM inference.”
Subhead: “Production-like chat + embeddings workloads across models and cloud regions, with variance reported.”
CTA: “Download report” + secondary “Explore region tables”.

Soojin Lee: tweak: “latency-per-dollar” might be too jargon. Maybe:
Hero: “Latency per dollar (production economics) benchmark for LLM inference.”
Subhead: “Measure how speed and cost trade off across models/regions—using a reproducible methodology.”

Tessa Morgan: I’ll update the wire to include a small inline definition tooltip:
“Latency/$ = p50 end-to-end latency normalized by $ spent for the run.”

Michael Grant: definition should avoid sounding like we are dividing one request by one request $ (since we use aggregated run cost). Suggest:
“Latency/$ is computed from measured p50 latency and metered cost over a standardized run window.”

Claire Dubois: yes, we compute from run aggregates (plus per-token cost). I’ll provide exact wording so docs don’t drift.

Ben Carter: can we align on an approval checklist so we stop thrashing on copy later?

Camila Reyes: yes. dropping checklist draft here — please add gaps.

Camila Reyes: APPROVAL CHECKLIST (headline stats + claims)
- Methodology sign-off: Jonas + Claire confirm the stat is supported by final QC table
- Baseline definition included wherever relative language appears (no “common” / “industry standard”)
- Variance language included near any superlatives (“up to”, “best observed”, etc.)
- Region/model scope stated (no implying global coverage if only NA/EU/APAC-1)
- Reliability wording: not an SLA; no uptime/error-rate headline unless explicitly labeled as “benchmark window observation”
- Legal review: Michael approves any comparative phrasing and disclaimers
- Design review: Tessa confirms chart + metric labels are unambiguous (units, axes, footnotes)
- Links: methodology appendix + FAQ linked from landing + PDF
- CTA consistency: Hosted API vs Dedicated/Private CTAs match field enablement talk track

Soojin Lee: add: “No single-number claim without a footnote link to the table row.” Even if it’s on the landing page.

Tyler Benson: add: “UTM tags present + consistent across channels” (I’ve seen us ship without them…).

Renee Sullivan: add: “Social pack uses the same approved phrasing; no one-off ‘we’re #1’ drafts.”

Michael Grant: add: “No competitor logos/names unless separately approved.” (Not expecting it, but good to lock.)

Claire Dubois: add: “Final QC pass complete (outliers resolved; reruns done; variance thresholds met).”

Ben Carter: perfect. I’ll update the landing wirecopy + PDF findings section today.
Action items:
- Ben: revise hero + remove ‘common hosted configs’ language; move 2.1× into PDF findings w/ baseline definition
- Claire/Jonas: send exact baseline definition + approved latency/$ definition text
- Michael: review revised hero + findings claim language once pasted into doc
- Tessa: update wire + tooltip + ensure footnote slot for any numeric callouts

Camila Reyes: thanks all. Let’s aim to have revised copy in the doc by EOD so we can unblock docs PR review tomorrow. :thumbsup:

(reactions: :thumbsup: from Soojin Lee, Ethan Wallace, Tyler Benson; :white_check_mark: from Michael Grant)
